Miserable describes a state of deep, heavy unhappiness or suffering — the kind that weighs on you, that you cannot easily shake off. It is far stronger than simply "sad" or "unhappy." When someone is miserable, they are not just a little down; they are in real distress, either emotionally or physically, or both.

Think of it this way: if "unhappy" is a cloudy day, "miserable" is a storm that won't stop.

Miserable is used in two main ways, and understanding both will give you full command of the word.

1. To describe how a person feels

This is the most common use. When a person is miserable, they are experiencing genuine suffering — emotional pain, physical pain, or a sense that everything feels hopeless and joyless.

  • She felt completely miserable after hearing the bad news.
  • He lay in bed, miserable with a fever and a sore throat.
  • I was miserable the entire time I lived in that city — I had no friends, no work, and no hope.

Notice that miserable can describe:

  • Emotional suffering — grief, loneliness, disappointment, heartbreak
  • Physical suffering — illness, discomfort, exhaustion
  • A general state of wretchedness — when life simply feels heavy and joyless

The key quality in all three is that the suffering is felt deeply and is not just a passing mood. It has weight and duration to it.

2. To describe things, conditions, or situations

Miserable can also describe things outside a person — weather, living conditions, a performance, a salary — to say that they are very bad, unpleasant, or completely inadequate. In this sense, the word means that whatever is being described either causes misery or is simply terrible in quality.

  • The weather was absolutely miserable — cold, wet, and grey for days.
  • They were housed in miserable conditions: no heat, no clean water, crumbling walls.
  • He gave a miserable performance — nervous, flat, and forgettable.
  • After all that work, they offered her a miserable sum of money. (meaning a pitifully small, inadequate amount)

Here, "miserable" does not mean the weather or the salary is "sad" — it means it is wretchedly bad, far below what is acceptable or decent. It often carries a sense of contempt or pity.
The Scale: How Strong Is This Word?

It helps to see miserable on a scale:

Unhappy → Sad → Miserable → Devastated

"Miserable" sits toward the more intense end. It is not the absolute worst a person can feel, but it suggests genuine, sustained suffering — not a momentary bad mood. There is often a sense of helplessness in it, a feeling that the person cannot easily escape their discomfort.
The Sense of "Pitifully Poor or Inadequate"

This is a sub-meaning worth knowing separately. When miserable is used to describe an amount, an attempt, or an effort, it means it falls so far below expectations that it is almost contemptible or pitiful.

  • The rescue team made a miserable attempt at saving the operation. (a very poor, weak attempt)
  • They survived on a miserable diet of bread and water. (an extremely inadequate diet)
  • He won the race by a miserable margin. — Actually, this is less common. More accurately: He earned a miserable wage. (embarrassingly low)

The idea here is: not just bad, but so bad that it is almost shameful or pathetic.

In British English especially, miserable is also used to describe a person who is consistently gloomy, grumpy, joyless, or unpleasant to be around — not because they are currently suffering, but because it seems to be their permanent nature.

  • Don't invite him — he's such a miserable man; he complains about everything.
  • Why are you being so miserable? It's a celebration!

This is close to calling someone a "grouch" or a "killjoy." The person is not necessarily in pain — they just seem to drain the joy out of every situation.

You will often hear or read "miserable" paired with these words:

  • feel miserable — the most natural phrase for personal suffering
  • look miserable — someone appears visibly distressed or downcast
  • miserable weather / day / night — unpleasant, grey, cold, wet
  • miserable life / existence — a life marked by ongoing hardship and suffering
  • miserable failure — a complete, embarrassing failure
  • miserable excuse — a very weak, unconvincing excuse
  • miserable conditions — very poor, inadequate living or working conditions
  • utterly / absolutely / completely miserable — these intensifiers are common because "miserable" already suggests intensity, and people often want to emphasise it further

• Miserable vs. sad: "Sad" is gentler and more neutral. "Miserable" implies deeper, more sustained suffering. You can feel sad at the end of a nice film; you feel miserable after a week of illness, loneliness, or loss.
  • Miserable vs. depressed: "Depressed" is more clinical and refers to a mental health condition or a very heavy, prolonged low. "Miserable" is more informal and situational — you can be miserable because of a cold, terrible weather, or a rough week. The two can overlap, but "miserable" is the everyday word and "depressed" carries more gravity.
  • Miserable vs. terrible/awful (for things): When describing situations or conditions, "miserable" often adds a human element — it implies that the conditions have an impact on someone's well-being or dignity, or that they are pathetically inadequate. "Terrible weather" is just bad weather; "miserable weather" feels more like the weather is making life harder to bear.
A Few Full Sentences Across Different Contexts

1. After the breakup, he spent weeks feeling utterly miserable, unable to eat or sleep properly. (emotional suffering)
  2. The children were miserable on the long journey — hot, bored, and cramped in the back seat. (physical discomfort)
  3. It had been a miserable winter — grey skies, constant rain, and biting cold. (conditions)
  4. The hotel room was miserable: damp walls, a broken heater, and a mattress on the floor. (quality and conditions causing distress)
  5. She received a miserable response to her application — not even a proper rejection letter. (pitifully inadequate)
  6. "Why is he always so miserable at parties?" she whispered. "He never smiles." (British English: gloomy personality)

Miserable means deeply unhappy or suffering (when describing people), very poor and unpleasant to the point of causing misery (when describing conditions or things), or pitifully inadequate (when describing efforts, amounts, or results) — and in some uses, it also describes a person who is permanently gloomy and unpleasant in character.
